note: Every piece of outside research the cell uses or rejected, with its sources, what the concept is in plain words, how and where we use it, and the evidence we produced ourselves. Media: links to the authors' project pages and videos (never copied), plus our own renders.

entries.title: Success Guided Sampling (A Balanced Data Diet)
entries.where: Isaac cell, PPO training (Phase 1, item 5 of the Isaac proposals)
entries.concept: During RL training, pick which task configuration to practise next from how often the policy has recently succeeded on it. A configuration with about 50 percent success teaches the most, so it is sampled most; a small floor keeps every configuration possible. Only the sampling changes; the optimiser is plain PPO.
entries.use: Our configuration bins are variant x connector pose and yaw x cable state x start phase x randomised physics. The sampler keeps the last 100 outcomes per bin with a beta weighting peaked at 0.5. Bank size 2,000 to 4,000 bins on the shared 5080 (our sizing, not published).
entries.evidence: Hardware result checked in the paper: UR5e zero-shot 94 percent gear mesh, 61 percent rod-in-hole, 37.5 percent nut-and-bolt (Table 2). Code not released as of 2026-10-14.

entries.title: AlphaNIST
entries.where: Isaac cell: one PPO policy across variants, binary reward, cached resets
entries.concept: One PPO policy learns all 20 NIST assembly tasks from a binary task-complete reward, with diverse cached reset states (OmniReset) and success-guided sampling. Adding shaped rewards made it worse.
entries.use: Reset snapshots along our expert runs and at every phase boundary become the start states; the reward is binary (sensor-based success detector, graded against truth). Simulation only in the paper: no hardware result.
entries.evidence: 98.2 percent training success across 20 tasks, 64K envs, 410 GPU hours (paper). Simulation only.

entries.title: OmniReset (UWLab)
entries.where: Isaac cell: reset-state generation, physics settings, controller
entries.concept: Generate many diverse reset states for assembly RL, train with an operational-space torque controller and identified arm dynamics, then transfer.
entries.use: Physics settings copied as our fast tier (dt 1/120, TGS, 192 position iterations, SDF where needed); controller identification by chirps (Isaac item 6); the reset snapshot method.
entries.evidence: Joint RMSE 7 deg with default dynamics to under 2 deg after identification (App. A.3).

entries.title: NVIDIA Factory, IndustReal, AutoMate, FORGE
entries.where: Isaac cell: contact settings, exploit guards, force observations, success head
entries.concept: A family of GPU assembly simulations and sim-to-real methods: fine signed-distance collision for tight clearances, an interpenetration measure that drops exploited samples (SAPU), force-threshold conditioning, and a learned early-termination success head trained with truth labels.
entries.use: Isaac Lab ships the Factory and FORGE environments; we copy the solver settings, the AutoMate interpenetration code, and the FORGE success head for our sensor-based detector (ruling 2026-10-14).
entries.evidence: Checked in code: dt 1/120, solver_type 1, 192 position iterations, contact offset 5 mm. FORGE success head real precision/recall 1.0 on the peg.

entries.title: ACCRUE: continual off-policy RL for robot foundation models
entries.where: Later: real-world fine-tuning of a pretrained policy per variant without forgetting
entries.concept: Fine-tune a robot foundation model (pi0.5, GR00T) on a new task with off-policy RL (FastTD3/FastSAC) while keeping earlier tasks: inherit the actor-critic from the previous task, learn the new one by interaction, and distil the old tasks from a replay buffer so they are not forgotten.
entries.use: Relevant once we have a pretrained policy and several variants to adapt on the real cell: it cuts robot interaction by 31 to 69 percent on AutoMate and NIST tasks in the paper and keeps 98.3 percent of prior-task success. Not for the first sim training (that is PPO with SGS). Code not released; revisit when it is.
entries.evidence: Numbers from the project page (2026-10-14); no uncertainty shown; code coming soon.

entries.title: TF-Gripper: Dynamixel force by current
entries.where: Servo tool design: why the pinch uses a load cell, not motor current
entries.concept: A Dynamixel gripper estimating grip force from motor current: measured deadband 0.45 N and 7 to 19 percent hysteresis.
entries.use: Ruled out current-based force for the servo tool; cell P reads the pinch instead.
entries.evidence: Numbers from the paper's Sec. III-A and App. A.

entries.title: Ling et al.: memory-updated FFC insertion with a tactile fingertip
entries.concept: A 3-axis magnetic tactile fingertip classifies lateral misalignment in 0.5 mm bands (97.9 percent) and a Bayesian memory retries with corrected offsets until insertion succeeds.
entries.use: We borrow the retry logic over our camera and force signals. The tactile sensor detects lateral offset only, not seating depth or latch closure, and does not fit the 30 x 6 mm pad.

entries.title: UMI-FT and CoinFT: cheap force sensing on grippers
entries.where: Justification for bar load cells on the servo tool
entries.concept: Low-cost force or force-torque sensing added to simple grippers is enough for contact-rich policies.
entries.use: Precedent for three $15 bar cells instead of a $7,000 six-axis sensor on the servo tool. CoinFT's 0.16 N error is too coarse for the seat bump, so we do not use it.

entries.title: RoboSimStudio: agentic real-to-sim on Newton
entries.where: Isaac cell ideas A (Newton-VBD cable in the stability test), B (force-feedback teleop for demos), C (video matching on hardware)
entries.concept: A coding agent builds a simulation of a real task from a phone video and a prompt, then humans and the agent tune physics with live sliders until it matches the video. Runs on Newton (MuJoCo-Warp for arms, VBD for cables).
entries.use: Three borrowed ideas; the toolkit itself is not adopted because its sim-to-real agreement is judged by eye and only one task was deployed.

entries.title: WireCraft: cable models in Isaac Lab
entries.concept: Isaac Lab cable models: articulated wire (12 segments, joint stiffness and damping 5.0) and an FEM wire (E 5e7 Pa, Poisson 0.49), friction 1 to 5.
entries.use: Seeds for our cable randomisation; verified on Isaac Sim 4.5 and 5.1, not 6.1.

entries.title: Lakshya's segmented D6 cable and solver settings
entries.concept: A flat cable as a chain of rigid segments joined by D6 spring joints, checked against a beam model to 1 percent; PGS 255 position iterations, physics at 8 kHz, control at 1 kHz; contact force from impulses.
entries.use: Our gold-reference cable tier; the fast tier must match its force traces.
entries.evidence: E005 numerical validation, E039/E040 runs (his repo).

entries.title: Isaac Lab 3.0 EA
entries.where: Isaac cell: vectorised environments and PPO trainers
entries.concept: NVIDIA's GPU-parallel RL framework on Isaac Sim; v3.0.0-EA (2026-09-16) matches Isaac Sim 6.1 and Python 3.12.
entries.use: Environments, PPO via rsl_rl or skrl; no LeRobot exporter, so we write one.

entries.title: Koch v1.1 and GELLO: low-cost Dynamixel hardware
entries.concept: Open low-cost arms and leaders built on Dynamixel XL330/XL430 servos used for imitation learning.
entries.use: Precedent for the XL330 in a learning gripper; GELLO pattern for the leader.

entries.title: Fotuhi and Bingul 2021: lead-screw parallel gripper
entries.concept: A stepper-driven lead-screw parallel gripper study.
entries.use: Precedent for a lead-screw parallel jaw.
